results.title: Port of Seattle Environmental Equity Map Orange
results.description:
Near-airport communities are some of the most diverse in King County, with over 95 spoken languages. Rich with cultural and ethnic diversity, these communities are also among the most historically under-served.

The Environmental Equity Index was established by the Port of Seattle's Office of Equity, Diversity, & Inclusion to develop equity-based partnerships and provide resources and support in these the most vulnerable communities within King County.

The Map consist of over 25 indicators within four categories; Environmental Exposures & Effects, Socioeconomic and Sensitive Populations. The combinations of all the categories helps score each of the census tracts within King County.

The census tracts are ranked between one and ten. One being the least impacted by it's environment and socioeconomic factors while ten being the communities most impacted. Such as, most impacted by linguistic isolation, heavy traffic pollution, or livable wage job access.

The first case study to use this Index was the South King County fund. The fund will award $10 million between 2019 and 2023 to address noise mitigation, environmental health and sustainability in near-airport cities, with a priority on Burien, Des Moines, Federal Way, Normandy Park, SeaTac, and Tukwila
results.snippet: The Port of Seattle Environmental Equity Map which displays the various historical disparities within King County.

Citywide GSI Project displays the data from CARTO.GSI_PT_PV.   The labels are based on the attribute PROJECT NAME. 

This data will not display when zoomed out beyond 1:3,000.

Seattle Executive Order 2013-01 and City Council Resolution 31459 direct City departments to coordinate to develop an implementation strategy for managing 700 million gallons of stormwater annually with green stormwater infrastructure approaches by 2025.  These data on the location, purpose, funder, install year, and best managed practices of GSI installations in Seattle are gathered and integrated for comprehensive Citywide tracking and reporting at the project level.

Updated weekly.

This hosted feature layer simulates a municipal urban forestry
inspection prioritization workflow.

Analysis includes

• Tree inventory QA/QC
• DBH estimation hierarchy
• Derived maturity classes
• Simulated inspection history
• Proximity to sidewalks
• Proximity to arterial streets
• Proximity to schools
• Proximity to trails
• Seattle Racial & Social Equity Index
• Weighted inspection priority model
• Five-year inspection scheduling

All condition ratings, inspection history, and maintenance
priorities are simulated for educational and portfolio purposes.

results.title: FROM HERE TO EVERYWHERE
results.description:
Non-Native settlers began sending natural resources out of Seattle to destinations around the world beginning in 1851. The first cargoes were logs cut from the hillsides and rolled into the water. Before long, timber, fish, and coal filled ship holds. This list is just a sampling of cargoes going to outside markets by the 1870s.

As the local population grew and trans-continental trains began service to Seattle, more imports came into the port. Seattle is the closest port to Asia in the continental United States. Seizing this advantage, shipping companies brought tea, raw silk, and consumer goods from Asian ports to Seattle’s piers and loaded them onto East Coast-bound trains.

results.title: Outside Citywide Public Space Data
results.description:
This is a comprehensive inventory of all outdoor public spaces in Seattle. It includes all types of publicly-accessible outdoor spaces (public parks, privately owned plazas, cemeteries, greenbelts, etc) across all forms of ownership (City of Seattle, the Port of Seattle, King County, universities, etc).

This dataset was developed for use in planning and analysis applications, and is oriented toward user experience. Therefore, areas under different forms of City ownership forming a connected open space have sometimes been merged, with all owners listed in the feature attributes (such as a greenbelt owned by both SPR and SDOT).

The dataset includes all outdoor publicly-accessible space (cemeteries, parks, schoolyards, etc). Buildings and parking lots are included in feature boundaries if the location is primarily dedicated toward environmental or outdoor recreational uses (such as a park). Buildings and parking lots are not included in locations primarily dedicated toward other uses (such as libraries and schoolyards). Waterbodies are included within feature boundaries only if they are surrounded by land-based public space.

PublicSpaceSeattle_EntryPts contains entrance points for the polygon features in this dataset.

Field definitions

NAME: name of public space

TYPE: public space type (i.e.. park, greenbelt, cemetery, golf course, plaza, etc)

OWNER: initials of owner (see OWNER NAME LONG for full name)

GREENSPACE: feature is or contains an occupiable lawn area

PLAYGROUND: feature is or contains a playground, play area, or play feature

SPORTS: feature is or contains a sports facility of any type, including a skatepark, basketball hoop, football field, etc

NATURAL: feature is or contains a natural area such as a forest or wetland

TRAIL: feature is or contains a trail network long enough to be used for walking, jogging, running, or biking (such as a loop trail within a large park, a segment of a larger trail network, etc)

AGRICULTURE: feature is used for or contains an area for agricultural activity, such as a community garden or p-patch

RESTROOM: feature contains a public restroom

WATER: feature contains or is in close proximity to a waterbody, stream, or human-made water feature. Does not indicate physical access.

PUBLIC ACCESS: y= unrestricted during daylight hours, limited=public access during limited hours (typically a schoolyard), no trails= no access due to a lack of trails (typically in a greenbelt), POPS=privately owned public spaces in which private security officers have discretion to limit access to certain people or populations, undeveloped= site has not been developed for public use yet, fee= there is an entrance fee

LARGER AREA NAME: name of public space, or name of larger area that the public space is a part of (i.e.. if three differently-named or distinct spaces form one contiguous public space)

COMBINED SIZE OF LARGER AREA: SF of feature or of larger area, if applicable

PUBLIC OR PRIVATE: ownership

OWNER TYPE: city, county, state, federal, private, school, npo, etc

OWNER LONG: full name of owner(s)

STATUS: open or planned (undeveloped)

MAINTAINED BY: entity primarily responsible to site maintenance

STEWARDS: other groups who contribute to the upkeep, restoration, or activation of the site

DATA SOURCE: where the feature data was originally pulled from

results.title: How Environmental Racism Reveals Injustices in Seattle, WA
results.description: The purpose of this tour is to divulge how environmental racism throughout history has been manipulated into a tool to further cultivate the City of Seattle's industrialization zones. Historical events like the Fort Lawton protest, have helped highlight the impacts of environmental racism and how it has caused the disproportionate health disparities of indigenous peoples, people of color, and lower-income communities. The greatest environmental impacts that are seen in the Duwamish Valley exist predominately in the lower parts, during annual sea level rises, which bring extreme flooding during high tide events in both residential and industrial riverfront lands. In 2001, the valley was classified as a federal superfund site, due to the 100 hazardous waste sites that heavily pollute the air and waterways with materials like PCBs, PAHs, arsenic, mercury, and phthalates (University of Washington, 2023). The valley is also bisected by three freeways, two rail lines, two airports, and a waterway corridor for marine freights. The very location and infrastructure for both the Port of Seattle, and the SoDo industrial site, reveal why disproportionate effects occur mostly within these lower-income neighborhoods like South Park and Georgetown.

results.title: Flood Risk in the Seattle Coastal Region
results.description:
Seattle’s booming population is one of the city’s defining features, being ranked 8th among the 50 densest cities in the United States. But this very urban sprawl, the rapid expansion of the city away from the core, sits uncomfortably close to the shoreline of Puget Sound, which is now under increasing threat from sea-level rise, according to local climate experts.

In a report covered by FOX 13 Seattle, Ian Miller, a coastal hazards specialist, warns that rising waters could push sea level in Seattle as much as two to three feet by the end of the century. These projections put not only isolated homes at risk, but also critical infrastructure, waterfront businesses, the ports and fisheries that drive the economy of the area.

The main area highlighted by Miller is South Park, a low-income neighborhood along the Duwamish River that flooded during a high tide event in December 2022. In that event, high tides led to flooding which ruined homes, roads, and businesses. Miller warns that such flooding could become “the new normal,” especially as sea level rises and groundwater levels, influenced by the ocean, push higher in areas farther from the shoreline.

results.name: Land_Cover_Forterra_2017
results.title: Land Cover Forterra 2017
results.description:
This dataset was developed using ArcGIS to perform a supervised classification on 2017 NAIP 4-band orthoimagery at a 1m resolution captured during the summer of 2017 and purchased from the USDA Aerial Photography Field Office.

A seamless mosaic was assembled for each of the four bands (red, blue, green, and near-infrared) as well as true color and false color composites. From the bands were derived a normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI), and two texture layers using a focal window with dimensions of 7x7 measuring the range of values within the window. These layers were averaged to create a single texture layer. 100 training polygons were digitized to identify areas corresponding to the following 11 classes:

  1. Developed/Impervious: Consists of buildings, roads, parking lots, and other forms of urban development

  2. Dry Grass: Grass that has little to no photosynthetic activity due to a lack of moisture and is less than 2’ in height

  3. Forest: Coniferous and deciduous trees that are over 15’ in height

  4. Irrigated Grass: Grass that is watered and has continued photosynthetic activity during the dry summer months and is less than 2’ in height

  5. Shadow over Developed/Impervious: Areas of cast shadows on developed/impervious features

  6. Shadow over Dry Grass: Areas of cast shadows over dry grass

  7. Shadow over Forest: Areas of cast shadows over forest

  8. Shadow over Irrigated Grass: Areas of cast shadows over irrigated grass

  9. Shadow over Water: Areas of cast shadows over water

  10. Shrubs: Coniferous and deciduous woody plants that are between 2’ and 15’ in height

  11. Water: Includes open water on Puget Sound, lakes, river channels, wetlands, and retention ponds.

Training polygons were selected using visual inspection of both true color and false color composites of the NAIP imagery in conjunction with Google Streetview images. The training polygons were converted to rasters, the rasters were used to create signature files, and the signature files were used to generate a maximum likelihood classification, using the R, B, G, NIR, NDVI, and texture rasters.

Vegetation was stratified according to height using 2016 LiDAR data obtained from King County using a vegetation height raster created by masking bare earth and first-return LiDAR data to the extent of the vegetated classes, then stratifying into: grass 0-2’, shrubs 2’-15’, forest 15+. Within wetland mitigation areas delineated by the Port of Seattle, a different stratification threshold was used to differentiate shrubs, with the upper limit set to 30’ to account for large willows within the wetlands.

After internal review of the preliminary classification the decision was made to combine several of our initial classes and to introduce a buildings a class, with the final set of classes consisting of:

• Buildings

• Developed/Impervious

• Dry grass/bare soil

• Forest

• Grass

• Shrub

• Water

Substantial effort was expended to improve the accuracy of the landcover classification. Over the course of four complete revisions to the initial classification, we used King County impervious surface data to improve and in many cases eliminate class confusion between developed/impervious and dry grass/bare soil, integrated vector building footprints and right-of-way data from the municipalities, and hand-digitized thousands of features such as buildings, retention ponds, areas of bare soil, and overwater structures on lakes. We applied the changes sequentially in order to minimize the liklihood of replacing overhanging tree canopy with these features.

results.title: The Best of the West
results.description: From the mountains and rainforests of the Pacific Northwest, across the rivers and lakes of the Intermontane region, to the bustling capitals of Mexamerica, the Best of the West roadtrip will explore several geographic regions across the western United States. Starting in the Pacific Northwest, we will visit Seattle, Washington, and Portland, Oregon, both prominent port cities along the Cascade Range known for diverse culture and natural beauty. In these cities, we will explore the mountains, forests, and rivers that make the Pacific Northwest by visiting Mount Rainier National Park and the Columbia River Gorge National Scenic Area . Heading west, we will explore the Intermontane region, often known for its arid climate and diverse landscapes. Here, we will stop in Boise, Idaho, and Salt Lake City, Utah, both large communities that blend urban centers with rich outdoor landscapes like the Boise River Greenbelt and the Great Salt Lake. We will end our trip in Mexamerica, examining how large urban landscapes meet unique deserts. Located in the Sonoran Desert, Phoenix, Arizona hosts a variety of outdoor and cultural activities, like Camelback Mountain and the Heard museum. We will then end our journey in Austin, Texas, a vibrant capital located on the Colorado River marked by its lush greenery in McKinney falls state park and live-music scene in the 6th street entertainment district.
results.snippet: Exploring the Western United States

results.title: The Long Haul into the West
results.description: This long road trip takes us across the Great Plains and Rocky Mountain region which is sprawled over many states, so the road trip has access to many different geological variations for physical landscapes as well as having access to the rich history within them. The trip starts in Rapid city South Dakota where you have access to Black Hills national forest then heading to Mt Rushmore since it's in the same state. This region leads perfectly into the next one being the Intermontane west and mexamerica region which holds a great geological phenomenon being the colorado plateau uplift which created many beautiful sceneries that are seen on the trip. The next stop will be Moab Utah which gives direct access to national parks such as arches and the city has their own museum to explain the history that's built into the walls of rock in the area. Next stop would be Las Vegas Nevada to see a more densely populated area compared to some of the others well also being surrounded by the Red Rock canyon with plenty of outdoor activities to do. From here the trip takes me northward to the Pacific NorthWest region for the first stop of Portland Oregon. This city has port access to the pacific ocean so there's historical battleships turned museums all around. Taking advantage of the high elevation that is in this region I plan to stop by Mount Hood which is the highest mountain in the state and lead you to the final stop of Seattle Washington and the state forest outside it. Within the city you get to see the oldest plane factory in the country at the red barn boeing museum.

results.title: Kingston Sub Area Plan
results.description:
Kingston is located on Appletree Cove, known for its sweeping views of Puget Sound and the Cascade and Olympic Mountain ranges. It is bordered by Port Gamble S’Klallam tribal land to the north, and rural residential properties to the south and west, with Puget Sound to the east. The community retains an authentic small-town character with multi-generational gathering places and businesses. The waterfront encompasses a large marina, public beach access and a major terminal for Washington State Ferries that is a key transportation link between the Seattle metropolitan area and the Olympic Peninsula.

The vision of Kingston focuses on the continued reservation and protection of open space, forests and critical habitat areas in the surrounding sensitive environment. Maintaining and improving public facilities for sewer and other utilities, stormwater management and emergency services is also envisioned. Guiding the preservation and development of diverse housing types for all incomes and ages will maintain an inclusive community. The Kingston community values its shoreline, parks and schools with interconnected systems of pedestrian and bicycle trails. Additional non-motorized facilities such as sidewalks, bike lanes and safe routes to schools will increase the health and safety of the community.

results.title: Kevin T. Cartography Portfolio
results.description:
I did the math...I've lived in 18 different houses in 31 years. With that much moving around, I got to see and experience a lot of the US, though some of it too young to comprehend all the splendor. My mother, a botanist and professor, instilled a curiousity in our natural resources and an interest in data that drives me to this day.

I graduated with a BS in Biology from James Madison University in 2015 and went on to complete my MS in Forest Resource Management at West Virginia University. I then hopped across the US to the Seattle area for nearly 5 years and worked primarily for local parks departments in invasive species management and forest restoration. Outside of a course here or there, I didn't have much exposure to GIS, though I saw it all around me. With the Parks Department, my true foray into GIS began. Leveraging Field Maps (Collector at the time), QuickCapture, and Dashboards, I revamped our tracking and monitoring system to better visualize our control efforts of invasive species across 25,000 acres, allowing us to make data-informed management decisions. I moved back to the east coast and landed in Philadelphia, PA, where I work as an environmental consultant. I perform tree inventories, wetland delineations, and other ecological assessments, then prepare technical reports and maps to convey data to managers and clients.
results.snippet: This is my digital portfolio—where my life story meets my passion for stewarding natural resources and leveraging data.
